summary:
FlameAtlas is a web dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into fire safety answers for crewed spacecraft, lunar and Martian habitats, and pressurized rovers.

We built a pipeline that reads NASA technical reports for PSI combustion investigations (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME BRE and others) and extracts 174 test records: fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity and outcome, each with a verbatim quote and page number. Users choose a crew environment, such as a Moon base at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psi, and FlameAtlas ranks the most similar real tests, maps flammability against oxygen and airflow, and bounds missing partial-gravity data with 0 g and 1 g results. An AI layer summarizes and interprets the evidence, citing a test or source page for every claim and stating plainly where the data stop.

This matters because fire limits measured on Earth can mislead in space. In BASS-II, PMMA kept burning at 13.6% O₂, below its 16% normal-gravity limit.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameAtlas is an interactive web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA microgravity combustion investigations from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database. It answers a practical question for engineers and researchers: given the atmosphere of my spacecraft or habitat, which real experiments are most relevant, and what do they say about fire risk?

HOW IT WORK
1. Collect. We gathered 15 NASA reports, papers and presentations (885 pages) for the PSI investigations most relevant to fire safety: BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I-VI, SAME, SAME-R, FLEX, FLEX-2 and ACME BRE, plus the ISS Researcher’s Guide to Combustion Science.
2. Extract. The pipeline reads text and tables from each PDF, including rotated test-matrix pages, and selects the data-rich pages of long reports. An LLM turns each test condition into a structured record: investigation, hardware, fuel and sample geometry, O2, pressure, airflow, gravity, outcome, spread rate and key finding. Every record keeps a verbatim quote and page number, and records are validated and normalized in code. The result is 174 test records, each linked to its PSI investigation page for citation by DOI.
3. Rank. Users pick a crew environment (ISS cabin, Moon base or pressurized rover at 30% O2 or more and 10.2 psi or less, Mars habitat, spacesuit) or set O2, pressure and airflow. A transparent similarity score ranks every test against those conditions. A catalog of 25 PSI combustion investigations ranks them by fire-safety relevance: prevention, detection or suppression.
4. Interpret. For the selected environment, the AI writes an insight card: risk level, what the experiments show, data gaps and design implications. Users can also ask questions in plain language or compare two investigations. The AI only sees the retrieved test records and document passages. It must cite a test ID or source page for every claim and say when the data do not answer a question. Below every answer, a table lists the cited tests with their quotes.
5. Bound partial gravity. PSI has no lunar or Martian gravity data yet, so the dashboard shows the closest microgravity and normal-gravity tests as bounds, as the challenge suggests.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Turns decades of scattered results into a searchable, comparable dataset in seconds instead of days of reading.
Every number traces back to a NASA source page, so engineers can trust and verify it.
Shows the evidence for higher-oxygen, lower-pressure exploration atmospheres, where materials become much more flammable. For example, in BASS-II PMMA sustained flame spread at 13.6% O2, below its 16% normal-gravity limit. Earth tests are not always conservative in space.
Helps researchers find gaps: untested conditions, missing partial-gravity data and investigations with little published detail.
Includes Earth applications from NASA fire research: water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection, firefighter breathing gear and protective clothing.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python, Streamlit (web app), Plotly (charts), PyMuPDF (PDF text and table extraction), Pydantic (data validation), pandas, a BM25 search index over 1,289 document passages, and the Claude API by Anthropic for extraction and interpretation. Data come from NASA PSI and the NASA Technical Reports Server. The code is on GitHub. No special hardware is needed.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a chatbot over PDFs, FlameAtlas builds a structured, citable test database first and uses AI only where it adds value. Ranking is deterministic and explainable. AI answers are grounded and traceable. The flammability map, which places each test by oxygen and airflow next to the user’s own environment, makes the danger zone visible at a glance. Bounding partial gravity with 0 g and 1 g data turns a missing dataset into an honest, useful estimate.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Trust: AI can be wrong, so every record and claim carries a quote and page, missing values stay empty rather than guessed, and each record has a confidence score.
Audience: professors, students, aerospace researchers and engineers, so we chose precise units and parameters over decoration.
Citation: each test links to its PSI investigation page, as PSI requires.
Scope: rocket and propellant combustion is excluded, as the challenge specifies.
Limits we state openly: 15 documents so far, sparse normal-gravity comparisons and no partial-gravity data in PSI yet.
